title: Asking for Freedom Makes Things Worse
overview: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go, and he answers by making their slave labor crueler, so the people turn on Moses and Moses turns to God with hard questions.

parts.label: The first demand (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Moses and Aaron bring the LORD's message, "Let my people go," and Pharaoh, honored in Egypt as a god-king, scoffs that he has never heard of this God and owes him nothing. His question about who this God is sets up the contest that the plagues in the following chapters will answer.

parts.label: A smaller request refused (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: They ask only for a three-day trip into the desert to offer sacrifices, but Pharaoh sees nothing except lost work and orders them back to their labor. Interpreters debate whether asking for just three days was a way of testing Pharaoh before the full demand, or a cover for leaving for good.

parts.label: Bricks without straw (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: Egyptian mud bricks were made with chopped straw mixed into the clay to hold them together, and until now the workers had been given it. Pharaoh orders them to find their own straw while making the same number of bricks, dismissing their wish to worship as nothing but a sign they have too little to do.

parts.label: Scattered and beaten (vv. 10-14)
parts.note: The workers spread across the countryside gathering leftover stubble from harvested fields, and they cannot keep up. The Israelite foremen, placed over their own people by the Egyptian slave drivers, are beaten for every shortfall.

parts.label: The foremen's failed appeal (vv. 15-21)
parts.note: The foremen protest to Pharaoh that the fault lies with his own people, but he only accuses them again of shirking work and sends them back. On the way out they blame Moses and Aaron for making them hated in Pharaoh's eyes, an idea the Hebrew puts as making their smell stink to him.

parts.label: Moses questions God (vv. 22-23)
parts.note: Moses brings his frustration straight to the LORD, asking why he was sent if things have only gotten worse and no rescue has come. The text lets the complaint stand without rebuke, and God's answer begins in the next chapter.

think: When an effort to make things better first makes them worse, what helps you decide whether to keep going or stop?
